Socoh (Shochoh)
SOH-koh
proper noun (place)
Hebrew Sokoh, a town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah; the staging-ground of the Philistines before the combat of David and Goliath.

📖 Biblical Definition

Socoh was a town in the Shephelah, the low hill country of Judah, best known as the place where the Philistines gathered their armies for the confrontation that brought David and Goliath face to face. "Now the Philistines gathered together their armies to battle, and were gathered together at Shochoh, which belongeth to Judah, and pitched between Shochoh and Azekah, in Ephesdammim" (1 Sam 17:1). There, in the valley of Elah between the two camps, the giant of Gath defied the armies of the living God morning and evening for forty days, until a shepherd boy came with his sling and five smooth stones, declaring, "the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands" (1 Sam 17:47). Socoh thus forms the backdrop of one of Scripture's greatest displays of faith over fear, of the LORD's power magnified through the weak and despised. The town appears also among the cities of Judah and as one of Solomon's commissary districts. Socoh stands in the dictionary as the place where the hosts of the uncircumcised mustered against Israel, and where God answered their champion's boast not with a greater giant but with a boy who trusted in the name of the LORD of hosts.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A town in the Judean lowland (1 Sam 17:1) where the Philistines mustered before the battle of David and Goliath in the nearby valley of Elah; the backdrop of faith's victory over the giant in the name of the LORD of hosts.

SOCOH (SHOCHOH), proper noun. A town in the Shephelah (lowland) of Judah.

Where the Philistines gathered their armies for battle (1 Sam 17:1).

Pitched between Shochoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim.

The backdrop of the combat of David and Goliath in the valley of Elah.

Also a town of Judah and a Solomonic commissary district.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Sam 17:1 — "Now the Philistines gathered together their armies to battle, and were gathered together at Shochoh, which belongeth to Judah, and pitched between Shochoh and Azekah, in Ephesdammim."

1 Sam 17:45 — "Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied."

1 Sam 17:47 — "And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands."

Josh 15:35 — "Jarmuth, and Adullam, Socoh, and Azekah,"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Socoh needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that the battle is the LORD's, won not by sword and spear but by faith in the name of the LORD of hosts.

expand to see more

Strength-trusting misreading. The Philistines at Socoh trusted in their giant, their armor, and their weapons; Israel trembled at the same. David reckoned by faith: the battle belongs to the LORD, who saves not with sword and spear. The dictionary holds the abiding lesson: the contests of God's people are not decided by visible might, and the believer who comes in the name of the LORD of hosts has on his side a power the strongest enemy cannot match.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is zeal for the honor of God's name. David's indignation rose not at personal insult but because the giant "defied the armies of the living God." The dictionary commends his motive: faith is moved most by the dishonor done to God, and acts for the vindication of His name. At Socoh the boast of the flesh fell before the boy who cared more for the glory of the LORD than for his own safety.
